extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Math 216 / Foundations of Algebraic Geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and computations of the blow-up of a closed subscheme in a scheme (including universal-property and Proj/Rees-algebra constructions), and uses such as resolving singularities and computing proper/total transforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal property characterization of blow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The blow-up Bl_X Y is defined by the universal property: it is a fiber diagram β: Bl_X Y -> Y with EXY (the scheme-theoretic pullback of X by β) an effective Cartier divisor, and any other such diagram (with D an effective Cartier divisor) factors uniquely through it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterization implies uniqueness up to unique isomorphism. It is the primary abstract definition used to show formal properties without computation; exercises and later proofs verify constructions satisfy this universal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional divisor is an effective Cartier divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: For the blow-up β: Bl_X Y -> Y, the preimage EXY (the scheme-theoretic pullback of X) is required to be an effective Cartier divisor on Bl_X Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition is central in the universal property and is used repeatedly (e.g., to show β is an isomorphism away from X); when X is locally principal the construction is explicit (Spec A/I example). The exceptional divisor is often denoted E and called the exceptional divisor of the blow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up is an isomorphism away from the center
rubrics_metrics.description: β|_{Bl_X Y - EXY} : Bl_X Y - EXY -> Y - X is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation 22.2.2 and related exercises emphasize that blowing up does not change the complement of the center; this is used in computations (e.g., proper transform equals closure of complement) and in the Blow-up Closure Lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case behaviors (empty/whole/Cartier center)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is empty then Bl_X Y = Y. If X = Y, then the blow-up is empty. If X ⊂ Y is an effective Cartier divisor then the blow-up is an isomorphism (id_Y : Y is the blow-up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These edge cases are immediate from the universal property and should be checked when reasoning about examples or inductive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locality of blow-ups (can compute locally)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U ⊂ Y is open, then Bl_{U∩X} U ≅ β^{-1}(U). Thus blow-ups can be computed locally on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.2.A and 22.2.B show reducing questions to affine/local computations; this underlies the explicit affine/Proj constructions and many example computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of irreducibility and reducedness
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is irreducible and X doesn't contain the generic point of Y, then Bl_X Y is irreducible. If Y is reduced, then Bl_X Y is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.2.C; useful when checking the blow-up stays within reasonable geometric classes (varieties), e.g., to deduce that blow-up of a k-variety is again a k-variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence for locally principal closed subschemes
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y is locally cut out by one equation (locally principal), then the blow-up Bl_X Y exists (reduce to affine Spec A/(t) ⊂ Spec A and construct Spec A/I as the blow-up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.2.4 outlines the affine construction and checks the universal property via ring arguments (Exercises 22.2.D–22.2.F). This geometric intuition: 'shaving off fuzz supported in V(t)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up Closure Lemma (proper transform computation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given W -> Z -> Y (closed embeddings) and blowing up Y along X, the proper transform of Z in Bl_X Y (scheme-theoretic closure of Z lowup^{-1}(W) ) is canonically isomorphic to Bl_W Z; similarly total transform is pullback. More precisely, (Bl_W Z, E_{WZ}) ≅ (Z, E_Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 22.2.6: this is the key computational tool: to blow up a subscheme of Z, one can blow up an ambient Y and then take the closure/proper transform. Many example computations (plane curves, nodes, cusps) use this repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj / Rees-algebra construction of blow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y corresponds to a finite-type quasi-coherent ideal sheaf I ⊂ O_Y, then Bl_X Y ≅ Proj_Y (⊕_{n≥0} I^n) (the Rees algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.2 gives the explicit construction used for computations and to prove existence generally. The degree-1 generation and finite-type hypotheses are important; this construction also identifies the exceptional divisor with Proj over X of the graded pieces I^n/I^{n+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up morphism is projective (hence proper, finite type, separated)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proj construction shows the blow-up morphism β: Bl_X Y -> Y is projective; consequently it is quasi-compact, proper, finite type, and separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to deduce global finiteness/properness properties in applications (e.g., resolution of singularities arguments requiring proper birational maps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional divisor description as Proj of associated graded (projectivized normal cone)
rubrics_metrics.description: EXY = Proj_X (⊕_{n≥0} I^n / I^{n+1}). Thus the exceptional divisor is the projectivization of the normal cone to X in Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula (22.3.2.1). When X is a regular embedding the exceptional divisor becomes a projective bundle (projectivized normal bundle). Exercises and examples explain how to read intersection data and multiplicities from this description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal cone and tangent cone definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal cone N_{X}Y is defined as Spec_X (⊕_{n≥0} I^n / I^{n+1}); for X a closed point this is the tangent cone to Y at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.3.6: think of this as an algebro-geometric tubular neighborhood; exercises show tangent-cone computations and their relation to exceptional divisors (projectivized tangent cone). Be cautious: N_{X}Y need not embed in Y even when smooth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-ups of regular embeddings are regular and have projective-bundle exceptional divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: If i: X ⊂ Y is a closed embedding of smooth varieties over k (regular embedding), then Bl_X Y is smooth; the exceptional divisor EXY is a projective bundle over X and the normal bundle to EXY restricts to O(-1) on fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.10 and consequences (22.3.8, 22.3.D): rely on the isomorphism In/In+1 ≅ Sym^n(I/I^2) when I generated by a regular sequence. Exercises show identifying the normal bundle and the projectivized normal bundle structure explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit affine/chart computation (plane blow-up example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blow-up of A^2 at origin can be described as Proj k[x,y,X,Y] with relation xY - yX = 0; on patches [X,Y]=[s,1] and [1,t] one gets Spec k[y,s] and Spec k[x,t] respectively, and the exceptional divisor is locally principal (cut out by y on one chart and x on the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.4.1 demonstrates how to compute charts, see exercises 22.4.A–22.4.C for using these charts to compute proper/total transforms of curves, multiplicities, and intersection with the exceptional divisor (slopes/tangents). Useful anti-pattern: forgetting to pass to appropriate charts when computing transform geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using blow-ups to partially or fully desingularize curves/surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a curve or surface singular at a point, taking the proper transform under the blow-up of the ambient space at that point can separate branches and sometimes resolve singularities (e.g., node y^2 = x^3 + x^2 becomes regular after blow-up; sequences of blow-ups resolve An singularities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 22.1 and 22.4 (exercises 22.4.B–22.4.F) show concrete examples: node, cusp, An singularities, and surface singularities z^2 = y^2 + x^{n+1}; Hironaka's theorem ensures resolution in characteristic 0 via sequences of blow-ups along regular centers. This provides a practical recipe: blow up singular points, take proper transform, iterate on remaining singular loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior when blowing up nonregular or nonreduced centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up a nonregular or nonreduced subscheme can produce singularities or do 'great violence' to the scheme; the result need not have the intuitive description available in the regular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns that in general blowing up can be destructive; Exercise 22.4.G shows blowing up the nonreduced subscheme V(y,x^2) in A^2 yields an A1 singularity. Hence one should check hypotheses (finite type ideal sheaf, regular embedding) before applying smoothness conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal bundle to a Cartier divisor and relation to blow-up normal bundle
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal bundle to a Cartier divisor D is the invertible sheaf O(D)|_D. In particular, for the blow-up of a point in the plane, the exceptional divisor has normal bundle O(-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.3.5 and Exercise 21.2.H: use this to identify which exceptional divisors can be blown down (Castelnuovo's criterion) and to recognize O(-1) behavior on projective-line exceptional divisors arising from point blow-ups on smooth surfaces.
